l: Israel's sin, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Israel's sin is described as perverse, wicked rebellion: turning aside from God's precepts, not listening to the prophets, and not entreating God's favor or turning from iniquity. Daniel acknowledges it brought the curse written in the law of Moses, and that God was righteous in bringing the evil.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, receives a true revelation about a great warfare and mourns for three weeks, abstaining from pleasant bread, meat, wine, and anointing. On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, by the river Hiddekel, he sees a man clothed in linen with a radiant, awe-inspiring appearance; his companions flee in terror while Daniel alone sees the vision and loses his strength. The man touches and strengthens Daniel, tells him he is greatly beloved, and says his words were heard from the first day he set his heart to understand. The man explains that the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood him twenty-one days until Michael came to help, and that he has come to explain what will happen to Daniel's people in the latter days. He says he will return to fight the prince of Persia, that the prince of Greece will come, and that only Michael, Daniel's prince, supports him against them.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, mourns for three weeks and then sees by the river Hiddekel a great vision of a man clothed in linen, which he alone sees. He falls on his face powerless, is touched and strengthened, and is told he is greatly beloved and that his words were heard from the first day he humbled himself to understand.

l: man clothed in linen, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: The man clothed in linen appears with thighs adorned with pure gold of Uphaz, a body like beryl, a face like lightning, eyes like flaming torches, arms and feet like burnished bronze, and a voice like a multitude. He tells Daniel he was sent because Daniel's words were heard, was withstood twenty-one days by the prince of Persia until Michael helped, and has come to explain what will happen to Daniel's people in the latter days. He strengthens Daniel and says he will return to fight the prince of Persia, after which the prince of Greece will come.

l: Michael, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Michael is described as one of the chief princes who came to help the speaker after the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood him for twenty-one days. He is called Daniel's prince and is said to be the only one who supports the speaker against the princes of Persia and Greece.

l: prince of Persia, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood the man clothed in linen for twenty-one days, until Michael came to help. The man says he will return to fight this prince, and that the prince of Greece will come when he goes out.

l: revelation, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, a revelation is revealed to Daniel, described as true and as a great warfare. Daniel understands it and has understanding of the vision. The man clothed in linen says he has come to make Daniel understand what will happen to his people in the latter days, and that the vision is yet for many days.

l: Daniel's mourning, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 10
s: Daniel mourns for three whole weeks, eating no pleasant bread, taking no meat or wine, and not anointing himself until the three weeks are fulfilled. The man clothed in linen later says that Daniel's words were heard from the first day he set his heart to understand and humble himself before God.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: Chapter 11 is a long prophetic account of conflict between the king of the south and the king of the north. It opens with kings of Persia and a mighty king whose kingdom is broken toward the four winds and not passed to his posterity. The two kings then trade alliances, invasions, and defeats, including a failed marriage agreement and campaigns into the glorious land. A contemptible person gains the kingdom by flatteries, deceives, and moves against the king of the south, then turns against the holy covenant, with forces profaning the sanctuary and setting up the abomination that makes desolate. The wise among the people instruct many and fall, and a self-exalting king magnifies himself above every god until the end, when the king of the north comes against him and then meets his end between the sea and the glorious holy mountain.

l: king of the north, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: The king of the north is repeatedly in conflict with the king of the south, being attacked by the southern king's successor, who carries off gods and treasures to Egypt, then returning with greater armies, taking a well-fortified city and standing in the glorious land. He gives the daughter of women to corrupt, but she does not stand for him. At the time of the end he comes like a whirlwind with chariots, horsemen and ships, overflows the countries and Egypt, is troubled by news from the east and north, and pitches his palace tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain before coming to his end with no one to help him.

l: king of the south, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: The king of the south is strong, and one of his princes becomes stronger and rules a great dominion. His daughter goes to the king of the north to make an agreement but fails to keep her strength. He is moved with anger and fights the northern king, gaining a multitude but not prevailing, and later loses a war against a great army because those who ate his delicacies devise plans against him. At the time of the end he contends with the self-exalting king.

l: contemptible person, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: The contemptible person stands up in the place of the tax-collector's kingdom, though the honor of the kingdom had not been given to him. He comes in a time of security and obtains the kingdom by flatteries, sweeps away overwhelming forces and the prince of the covenant, and after a treaty works deceitfully while becoming strong with a small people. He scatters plunder, plots against strongholds, attacks the king of the south, and then directs his heart and actions against the holy covenant after ships of Kittim oppose him.

l: holy covenant, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: The holy covenant becomes the object of hostility when the king returns to his land with great wealth and his heart is against it. He has indignation against it, takes action, and favors those who forsake it. His forces profane the sanctuary, remove the continual burnt offering, and set up the abomination that makes desolate, while he corrupts covenant-breakers by flatteries.

l: wise among the people, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: The wise among the people instruct many, yet fall by sword, flame, captivity and plunder for many days. When they fall they receive a little help, while many join them with flatteries. Some of the wise fall to refine, purify and make them white until the time of the end, which is still for the appointed time.

l: self-exalting king, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 11
s: The self-exalting king does according to his will, magnifies himself above every god, and speaks marvelous things against the God of gods. He prospers until the indignation is accomplished, disregards his fathers' gods and the desire of women, and honors a god of fortresses unknown to his fathers with gold, silver and precious things. With a foreign god's help he deals with strong fortresses, increases the glory of those who acknowledge him, makes them rule over many, and divides the land for a price.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 describes the end-time events revealed to Daniel. Michael, the great prince who stands for Daniel's people, will arise during an unprecedented time of trouble, when everyone found written in the book will be delivered. Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and contempt, and the wise and those who turn many to righteousness will shine like the expanse and the stars. Daniel is told to shut up and seal the words until the time of the end, and he sees two others on the river banks ask the man clothed in linen how long until the end; the man swears by him who lives forever that it will be a time, times, and a half. Daniel does not understand, is told the words remain sealed, and is given the figures of 1,290 and 1,335 days before being told to go his way and that he will rest and stand in his inheritance at the end of the days.

l: Michael, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: Michael is called the great prince who stands for the children of Daniel's people. He will stand up at the time of trouble, and at that time the people will be delivered.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. He looks and sees two others on the river banks, hears the man clothed in linen swear an oath but does not understand it, and asks about the outcome. He is told to go his way, and that he will rest and stand in his inheritance at the end of the days.

l: man clothed in linen, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: The man clothed in linen is above the waters of the river and is asked by one of the two others how long until the end of these wonders. He raises both hands to heaven and swears by him who lives forever that it will be a time, times, and a half, and that all will be finished when the breaking of the power of the holy people is complete.

l: people of Daniel (your people), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: Daniel's people are said to be delivered at the time of trouble, everyone who is found written in the book. Michael stands for them.

l: those who sleep in the dust of the earth, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake. Some will awake to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

l: the wise, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: The wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse, and those who turn many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever. They will understand the things that the wicked do not understand.

l: time of trouble, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: The time of trouble is described as one such as never was since there was a nation. It occurs when Michael stands up, and the people are delivered during it.

l: sealed book (Daniel's words), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: Daniel is commanded to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. He is told again that the words are shut up and sealed until then, though many will run back and forth and knowledge will increase.

l: time of the end, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 12
s: The time of the end is the point until which Daniel's words remain sealed. It is marked by increased knowledge, the purifying of many, the wicked doing wickedly, and the 1,290 and 1,335 day periods from the removal of the continual burnt offering and the setting up of the abomination that makes desolate.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: Joakim, a rich man of Babylon, has a beautiful and God-fearing wife, Susanna. Two elders who serve as judges lust after her, hide in Joakim's garden, and threaten to accuse her of adultery with a young man unless she lies with them. Susanna refuses and cries out, and the elders publicly accuse her, and the assembly condemns her to death. As she is led away, Daniel cries out that he is innocent of her blood, has the elders separated, and questions each about the tree under which they saw her, and their conflicting answers (a mastick tree and an evergreen oak) expose their lie. The people bless God, put the elders to death according to the law of Moses, and Susanna's family praises God while Daniel gains a great reputation.

l: Susanna, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: Susanna, daughter of Helkias and wife of Joakim, is a very fair woman who fears the Lord and was taught the law of Moses. When the two elders threaten her in the garden, she refuses them, preferring to fall into their hands rather than sin before the Lord, and she cries out. She is falsely accused and condemned to death, prays to God, and is saved when Daniel exposes the elders' lie.

l: Joakim, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: Joakim is a great rich man of Babylon, married to Susanna, with a beautiful garden next to his house. The Jews come to him because he is more honorable than all others, and the elders-judges frequent his house. After Susanna is vindicated, he joins her parents and kindred in praising God.

l: two elders, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: The two elders, appointed judges that year, become inflamed with lust for Susanna, secretly watch her, and hide in the garden to ambush her. When she refuses, they falsely accuse her of lying with a young man, and the assembly believes them and condemns her. Daniel separates and questions them, they name different trees, and the assembly puts them to death according to the law of Moses.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: Daniel is a young youth whose holy spirit God raises up as Susanna is led to execution. He declares himself clear of her blood, rebukes the people for condemning her without examination, and examines the elders separately about the tree under which they saw the couple. Their contradictory answers prove the false testimony, and from that day Daniel has a great reputation among the people.

l: garden (Joakim's garden), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: The garden is the beautiful one next to Joakim's house, where Susanna walks at noon after the people depart. The two elders hide there and, once her maids have shut the doors and gone, confront her. It is the site of the alleged adultery, with the elders claiming to have seen it under a tree.

l: the people, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: The people assemble at Joakim's house and believe the elders' testimony, condemning Susanna to death. When Daniel challenges them, they return in haste to the place of judgment. After the elders' lie is exposed, they cry out, bless God who saves those who hope in him, and put the elders to death.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: The Lord is the God whom Susanna fears and trusts, and before whom she refuses to sin. He hears her cry as she is condemned and raises up Daniel to save her. The Lord's command that the innocent and righteous not be killed is cited by Daniel, and the people bless God for saving those who hope in him.

l: young man (alleged lover), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: The young man is an invented figure whom the two elders claim they saw lying with Susanna in the garden. They say he was stronger than they, opened the doors, and leaped out, and that Susanna would not name him. Daniel's examination shows that the story, and so the young man, was a lie.

l: trial of Susanna, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 13
s: The trial takes place before the assembled people at Joakim's house, where the elders have Susanna unveiled, lay hands on her head, and testify against her. The assembly believes them as elders and judges and condemns her to death. Daniel reopens the case, exposes the false testimony through separate questioning, and the sentence falls on the elders instead.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: After King Astyages dies and Cyrus the Persian takes his kingdom, Daniel, honored by the king, refuses to worship the idol Bel and proves it eats nothing by scattering ashes on the temple floor, where the footprints of Bel's seventy priests and their families reveal their secret entrance. The king kills the priests and gives Bel and its temple to Daniel, who destroys them. Daniel then kills the worshiped dragon of Babylon by feeding it lumps of pitch, fat, and hair, which enrages the Babylonians, who threaten the king until he hands Daniel over. Daniel is thrown into the lions' den for six days, where the prophet Habakkuk is carried by the angel of the Lord from Jewry to bring him a meal. On the seventh day the king finds Daniel alive, praises Daniel's God, and casts Daniel's accusers into the den, where the lions devour them.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: Daniel lives with the king and is honored above his friends, but worships only the living God and refuses to worship Bel. He exposes the priests' deceit with ashes, destroys Bel and its temple, kills the dragon with lumps of pitch, fat, and hair, and is handed over to the Babylonians and thrown into the lions' den. He is fed by Habakkuk's delivered dinner, is found alive on the seventh day, and is drawn out by the king.

l: Bel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: Bel is a Babylonian idol, clay inside and brass outside, to which large amounts of flour, sheep, and wine are given daily. Daniel shows that it never eats or drinks, and the king hands it over to Daniel, who overthrows it and its temple.

l: Cyrus the Persian, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: Cyrus the Persian receives the kingdom after Astyages is gathered to his fathers, honors Daniel, and at first worships Bel and believes it is a living god. After Daniel exposes the priests, he kills them and gives Bel to Daniel, but later yields to the Babylonians' threats and delivers Daniel to them. On finding Daniel alive in the den, he praises the Lord, the God of Daniel, and has Daniel's accusers thrown to the lions.

l: priests of Bel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: The seventy priests of Bel, with their wives and children, secretly enter through a hidden entrance under the table each night and consume the food and wine offered to Bel. Ashes scattered by Daniel's servants reveal their footprints, and the king kills them after they show him the secret doors.

l: dragon (of Babylon), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: The great dragon is worshiped by the people of Babylon, and the king presents it as a living god because it eats and drinks. Daniel feeds it lumps of melted pitch, fat, and hair, and it eats them and bursts apart.

l: Babylonians, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: The people of Babylon worship the dragon and, enraged by the destruction of Bel, the dragon, and the priests, accuse the king of having become a Jew. They threaten to destroy the king and his house unless he delivers Daniel to them, and he does.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: God is the living God who created the sky and the earth and has sovereignty over all flesh, whom Daniel worships. He sends dinner to Daniel in the lions' den through Habakkuk and the angel, and the king praises him as the God of Daniel, beside whom there is none other.

l: Habakkuk, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: Habakkuk is a prophet in Jewry who has made stew and bread to take to the reapers in the field. At the angel's command he is carried by the hair to Babylon and the den, calls to Daniel to take the dinner God has sent, and is then immediately returned to his own place.

l: angel of the Lord, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: The angel of the Lord tells Habakkuk to carry his dinner to Daniel in the lions' den in Babylon. He lifts Habakkuk by the hair of his head and sets him over the den with the blast of his breath, then returns him to his own place immediately.

l: lions' den, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 14
s: The den holds seven lions that are normally given two carcasses and two sheep daily, but are given none so that they will devour Daniel. Daniel stays there six days unharmed and is found sitting alive on the seventh day, after which his accusers are thrown in and devoured at once.

l: Tobit
s: The document is the Book of Tobit, a narrative in fourteen chapters about a righteous Naphtali exile in Nineveh, his family, and God's intervention through the angel Raphael. Tobit, carried captive from Thisbe in the days of Enemessar, stays faithful to the law, gives alms, and buries slain Israelites. After Sennacherib's reign he is informed on, loses his goods, and is later restored through his kinsman Achiacharus. He then buries another murdered man, is blinded when sparrow dung falls in his eyes, and is rebuked by his wife Anna over alms. Grieved, he prays for death. On the same day in Ecbatana, Sarah, daughter of Raguel, whose seven husbands were killed by the demon Asmodaeus, prays likewise. Both prayers are heard, and Raphael is sent to heal Tobit, give Sarah to Tobias, and bind the demon. Tobit instructs his son Tobias about burial, alms, marriage within the kindred, and ten talents of silver left with Gabael in Rages of Media. Tobias hires a companion who claims to be Azarias, actually Raphael, and travels with him and his dog. At the Tigris a fish is caught; its heart and liver are kept to drive off demons and its bile to heal eyes. At Ecbatana Raguel recognizes Tobias as Tobit's kin and gives him Sarah under a contract. Tobias burns the heart and liver, the demon flees to Egypt and is bound, and the couple survive. Raphael fetches the money from Gabael while a fourteen-day feast is held. Tobias leaves with Sarah and half of Raguel's goods. Anna, who has been waiting anxiously, sees him coming. Tobias anoints Tobit's eyes with the bile and restores his sight. Tobit offers Raphael half the goods, and Raphael reveals his identity as one of the seven holy angels, urges thanks to God, tells them to record events, and ascends. Tobit then writes a prayer of praise, foretelling Israel's regathering and a glorious rebuilt Jerusalem. In his last charge he tells his family to leave Nineveh before its prophesied fall, foretells Jerusalem's destruction and restoration, and urges righteousness. Tobit dies at 158. Tobias buries him and Anna, moves to Media, and dies at 127 after hearing of Nineveh's destruction.

l: Tobit, Tobit
s: Tobit is a righteous man of the tribe of Naphtali, son of Tobiel and descended from Asiel, carried captive from Thisbe to Nineveh in the days of Enemessar. He walks in truth and righteousness, gives alms, tithes and offerings, and alone of his tribe goes to Jerusalem for the feasts. He is married to Anna, father of Tobias, refuses the Gentiles' bread, and becomes Enemessar's purchasing agent, with favor granted by the Most High. He leaves ten talents of silver in trust with Gabael at Rages of Media. His habit of burying slain kinsmen brings an informer's charge, flight, and the loss of all goods except his wife and son, until his nephew Achiacharus helps him return to Nineveh. After burying a strangled kinsman at a Pentecost feast, he is mocked by neighbors, sleeps by his courtyard wall, and loses his sight to sparrow dung, at age fifty-eight. Poor and dependent on Achiacharus, he quarrels with Anna over a kid she brought home. Grieved, he prays for death, confessing God's righteous judgments, and his prayer is heard as Raphael is sent to heal him. He instructs Tobias in righteousness, alms and fearing God, hands over the handwriting for the money, and hires a companion, whom he accepts as kindred, promising wages and assuring Anna a good angel will go with their son. While Tobias is delayed he worries but insists the boy is well. On his return Tobias rubs bile on his father's eyes, the white films peel away, and Tobit sees, blesses God, and publicly gives thanks. He insists the companion be paid, then falls in fear when Raphael is revealed, and is told to bless God and write down what happened. He writes a prayer of rejoicing, exalting God as everlasting King and urging sinners to repent. In old age he charges Tobias and his six grandsons to leave Nineveh, keep the law, and bury him and Anna. He dies at 158 and is buried magnificently, with Anna, by Tobias. Overall his story moves from faithful suffering and affliction to mercy, restored sight, and thanksgiving.

l: Gabael, Tobit
s: Gabael, son and brother of Gabrias, lives at Rages of Media and holds ten talents of silver Tobit left in trust. Tobit fears he may be dead, but when Raphael lodges with him and presents the handwriting, Gabael produces the sealed bags, hands them over, and travels with Raphael to the wedding feast.

l: Enemessar, Tobit
s: Enemessar, king of the Assyrians, held Tobit captive yet favored him as purchasing agent through God's grace; upon his death his son Sennacherib succeeded him.

l: Nineveh, Tobit
s: Nineveh is the Assyrian city where Tobit and his people were held captive and where he buried dead Israelites. Jonah's prophecy foretells its overthrow; Tobit warns his family to leave, then rejoices hearing Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus destroyed and captured it.

l: Jerusalem, Tobit
s: Jerusalem is the holy city chosen out of all Israel's tribes for sacrifice, containing the temple of the Most High, hallowed for all ages, and the altar where priests received offerings. Tobit alone of his tribe went often to its feasts with first fruits and tithes. It is then foretold that Jerusalem will be scourged for its sons' works and desolate for a time, but God will show mercy, bring the people back from captivity, and have it rebuilt with honor, its tabernacle restored with joy, adorned with precious stones and gold. Many nations will come with gifts, and God exalts it forever.

l: God, Tobit
s: God is portrayed as the eternal Lord, the Holy One, and the everlasting King of heaven, who dwells in heaven with holy angels, gives all good things, and is Lord and Father of the children of Israel forever. Early on, the records stress his dual action toward Israel: he scatters them among the Gentiles and scourges Jerusalem for the works of her sons, yet shows mercy and brings them back to the land. In Chapter 3 he is addressed as righteous, true in judgment, and hears the prayers of Tobit and Sarah, sending Raphael to heal both. Chapter 4 tells Tobias to remember and bless him always, noting he humbles whom he will and does not turn his face from those who help the poor. In Chapter 11 Tobias and Tobit bless him for the journey's success and for restoring Tobit's sight after scourging. Chapter 12 reveals his works, says the Holy One received the memorial of their prayers, and Raphael ascends to him. Chapter 13 praises him as the one who scourges and shows mercy, will gather the scattered, and will exalt Jerusalem forever. Chapter 14 foretells renewed mercy, a return to the land, and all nations turning to fear and bless him.

l: Anna, Tobit
s: Anna is the wife of Tobit, the narrator, and mother of Tobias. She earns wages weaving cloth in the women's chambers, and when her husband doubts the kid she was given, she sharply rebukes him. Her devotion centers on her son: she weeps when Tobias is sent away, valuing him above money, until Tobit reassures her. Later she watches the path for him, spots his return, runs to embrace him, and says she is ready to die, weeping together.

l: Tobias, Tobit
s: Tobias is the young man and only son of Tobit and Anna, the dutiful heir whose story is one of obedience, marriage and healing. He is first seen as the son restored to his father at the Pentecost feast, sent to find a poor kinsman for dinner, and he reports a man of their race strangled and cast out in the marketplace. Sarah is destined for him, and it belongs to him to inherit her. Tobit instructs him to bury him, honor his mother, give alms, and marry within the kindred, and tells him of ten talents of silver held by Gabael. Tobias promises obedience, finds a companion, Raphael (whom he does not know is an angel and calls Brother Azarias), and sets out with his dog following. At the Tigris he seizes the leaping fish and keeps its heart, liver and bile. He fears dying like Sarah's seven previous husbands, being an only son, but the angel reassures him, and he comes to love Sarah. At Raguel's house, a kinsman's, he refuses to eat until a covenant is made, then receives Sarah as wife. He burns the heart and liver to drive off the demon, leads his bride in prayer asking mercy and to grow old with her, and takes a wife for truth, not lust. Bound by Raguel's oath to stay fourteen days, he sends Raphael to Gabael for the money, worrying that his father, counting the days, will grieve. After the feast he insists on going home and receives Sarah and half of Raguel's goods. Running ahead to Nineveh with the bile, he anoints Tobit's eyes, saying 'Cheer up, my father,' and restores his sight, then reports events in Media. He proposes giving the companion half of all he brought, and falls on his face in fear when Raphael is revealed; he and Tobit then confess God's works. At the end he receives Tobit's final instructions, buries Tobit and Anna, and moves with his wife and sons to Ecbatana. There he grows old in honor, buries his parents-in-law, inherits their possessions and his father's, and dies at 127 after hearing of Nineveh's destruction.

l: Media, Tobit
s: has_prospect peace for a season [contrasted with Nineveh's overthrow] Tobit directs Tobias to go into Media, where he believes there will be peace for a season rather than the overthrow coming on Nineveh. Tobias settles at Ecbatana of Media, where he grows old and dies.

l: Sennacherib, Tobit
s: Sennacherib, son and successor of Enemessar, ruled in troubled times, killing many Israelites fleeing Judea in his wrath and seeking Tobit to execute him. Fifty-five days later two of his sons murdered him and fled to Ararat; Sarchedonus reigned.

l: Achiacharus, Tobit
s: Achiacharus, son of Tobit's brother Anael, was appointed by Sarchedonus over the kingdom's accounts and affairs, serving as cupbearer, signet-keeper and steward next to the king; he escaped Aman's plot and requested Tobit, who came to Nineveh.

l: ten talents of silver (Tobit's silver), Tobit
s: Ten talents of silver were left in trust by Tobit with Gabael at Rages of Media. Tobit explains the deposit to Tobias, stressing that fearing God is true wealth. Tobias worries he doesn't know the holder, so Tobit gives him the handwriting. Raphael later presents it for Tobias, Gabael hands over the sealed bags, and the money is carried back toward the wedding feast.

l: alms, Tobit
s: Alms, the giving of bread to the hungry and garments to the naked, is presented in Tobit as a practice of great spiritual worth. It begins with Tobit's own generosity to kindred and nation, including a third tenth commanded by his father's mother Deborah. He then urges Tobias to give according to his abundance, or even from a little, without an envious eye. Alms is called a good gift before the Most High and a good treasure laid up against necessity. Raphael teaches it is better than laying up gold, delivers from death, and purges away all sin. Finally Tobit cites Manasses, who escaped the snare of death by giving alms, while Aman perished, and Tobit himself gave alms after his sight was restored.

l: burial of the dead (Tobit's burying), Tobit
s: Tobit buried any of his race found dead and thrown out on the wall of Nineveh, and privately buried those Sennacherib killed after they fled from Judea. When a Ninevite told the king, Tobit hid and withdrew in fear, and all his goods were forcibly taken.

l: poor man (kinsman of the narrator), Tobit
s: is_a strangled kinsman cast out in the marketplace The poor man is a member of the narrator's race who has been strangled and cast out in the marketplace. The narrator takes him up into a chamber until the sun sets and then buries him.

l: burial of the strangled man, Tobit
s: has_location grave dug by the narrator [after sunset] After sunset the narrator digs a grave and buries the strangled kinsman, weeping. His neighbors mock him, saying he is no longer afraid of being put to death for this and yet buries the dead again.

l: sparrows, Tobit
s: lives_in wall of the narrator's courtyard Unknown to the narrator, sparrows nested in the wall of his courtyard where he slept. Their warm dung fell into his open eyes and caused white films to form.

l: white films (Tobit's eyes), Tobit
s: White films blind the narrator after sparrows' dung falls into his eyes while he sleeps by a wall; physicians fail, Achiacharus sustains him, and after eight years sight returns.

l: kid (Anna's kid), Tobit
s: is_a gift given with wages [given to Anna by the owners] The kid is given to Anna along with her wages for weaving, and it cries when it reaches the house. The narrator suspects it is stolen and insists it be returned to the owners, while Anna says it was a gift beyond her wages.

l: Sarah, Tobit
s: Sarah is the fair and wise only daughter of Raguel and Edna, living in Ecbatana of Media in the land of her captivity. She has been given to seven husbands, all of whom perished in the bride-chamber, and her father's maidservants reproach her for it. Grieved enough to think of hanging herself, she desists to spare her father sorrow. She prays by the window, claims purity from all sin with man, and asks to be released from the earth or shown pity. Her prayer is heard: she was prepared for Tobias from the beginning, and as a kinswoman whose inheritance falls to him, she is to be his wife. She meets the travelers and brings them into the house, and her father gives her to Tobias. She is led away weeping, comforted by her mother. In the bride-chamber she joins Tobias's prayer with 'Amen' and sleeps through the night alive, to the maidservant's discovery. Raguel then gives her to Tobias with half his goods, tells her to honor her parents-in-law, and Edna commits her to Tobias's care. Arriving near Nineveh, she is welcomed by Tobit as daughter and blessed, ending her story in a new family.

l: Raguel, Tobit
s: Raguel is a man living in Ecbatana, husband of Edna, cousin of Tobit, and father of an only daughter, Sarah. Bound by the law of Moses, he may marry Sarah only to Tobias, her kinsman with the inheritance, on pain of death. He receives Tobias, recognizes his resemblance to Tobit, and weeps at Tobit's blindness. He admits seven earlier husbands died in the night, yet gives Sarah to Tobias and seals a contract. Fearing Tobias will die, he digs a grave, but after learning he lives he blesses God, has it filled, and holds a fourteen-day wedding feast. He swears Tobias must stay until it ends. He promises half his goods, the rest after his and his wife's deaths. At departure he yields to Tobias's insistence, gives Sarah and half his goods, servants, cattle and money, blesses them, instructs Sarah to honor her in-laws, and kisses her.

l: Asmodaeus, Tobit
s: Asmodaeus is an evil spirit who loves Sarah and killed her seven husbands in the bride-chamber before they lay with her. Raphael is sent to bind him because Sarah belongs to Tobias; the fish's smoke will make him flee, never returning.

l: Raphael, Tobit
s: Raphael is an angel, one of the seven holy angels who present the saints' prayers before God's glory, sent by God to heal Tobit and Sarah. His tasks are to scale the white films from Tobit's eyes, give Sarah to Tobias as wife, and bind the evil spirit Asmodaeus. He first appears in disguise: Tobias does not recognize him, and he claims the name Azarias, son of Ananias the great, of Tobit's kindred. Saying he knows the way to Rages of Media well and has lodged with Gabael, he is hired at a drachma a day plus necessities and becomes Tobias's companion, addressed as Brother Azarias. He travels with Tobias to Ecbatana and presents the matter discussed on the road to Raguel. Later he takes a servant and two camels to Gabael in Rages, collects the sealed bags of money, and brings Gabael back to the wedding feast. Near the end he urges Tobias to run ahead and carry the fish's bile, and instructs him to anoint Tobit's eyes so the films fall away. Offered half of all that was brought, he reveals his identity, explains he brought the memorial of Tobit's and Sarah's prayers, and says he only appeared to eat and drink. He tells them to write everything in a book, then ascends to God and is seen no more.

l: seven men (Sarah's previous suitors), Tobit
s: Seven kinsmen of Raguel to whom Sarah was given in marriage; each was killed by Asmodaeus on entering her room before consummation, leading maidservants to accuse Sarah and causing her reproach, despair, and later Raguel's admission.

l: Tobit's prayer, Tobit
s: is_heard_by Lord [heard before the glory of the great God] Tobit's prayer praises the Lord's righteous judgments and asks that he not be punished for his sins and those of his fathers, who were given over to plunder, captivity, death, and reproach among the nations. He asks that his spirit be taken so he may be released from distress and go to the everlasting place. It is heard before the glory of God.

l: Sarah's prayer, Tobit
s: is_heard_by Lord [heard before the glory of the great God] Sarah's prayer, made by the window, blesses the Lord's name and asks that she be released from the earth and hear no more reproach. She declares herself pure from sin with man and notes she is her father's only daughter with no heir. If death is not pleasing to God, she asks for regard and pity. It is heard before the glory of God.

l: Rages of Media, Tobit
s: Rages of Media is a place that is the destination of Tobias's journey, where money is to be collected. Raphael knows the way; Gabael is there. Raphael travels there, lodges with Gabael, collects the bags, and returns for the wedding feast.

l: marriage within kindred, Tobit
s: Marriage within kindred is a practice of Tobit's ancestors Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were blessed in their children and whose seed inherited the land; Tobit urges Tobias to marry within his father's tribe, not scorn kindred.

l: righteousness, Tobit
s: results_in prosperous success [for those who do righteousness] Tobit instructs Tobias to do righteousness all the days of his life and not follow the ways of unrighteousness. He says that those who do what is true will see their deeds prosper, and that doing what pleases God and departing from sin brings true wealth.

l: wages of the angel (Raphael's wages), Tobit
s: Raphael's wages are half of all Tobias brought back, proposed by Tobias and agreed by Tobit as due; the angel is told to take it, but Raphael gives no recorded response, instead teaching and revealing himself.

l: journey to Rages (Tobias's journey), Tobit
s: is_protected_by God [his angel is to go with Tobias] Tobias finds a companion for the journey, and Tobit hires him at a drachma a day with necessities and a promised addition if both return safe. Tobias prepares, and he and Raphael depart with the dog after Tobit's blessing that God and his angel will prosper the way. Tobit assures Anna that the journey will be prospered and Tobias will return safe and sound.

l: Azarias, Tobit
s: Azarias is an angel who travels with Tobias as guide and companion, addressed as brother. In Chapter 6 he has Tobias keep the fish's heart, liver and bile, explains their uses, proposes Sarah as bride, and promises God's salvation.

l: fish (in the Tigris), Tobit
s: A fish from the Tigris leaps to swallow Tobias, but at the angel's command he hauls it ashore; its heart, liver and bile are kept, and the rest is roasted and eaten.

l: incense ashes and fish heart and liver (Tobias's smoke), Tobit
s: Fish heart and liver, kept by Tobias on the angel's order, serve as a remedy against demonic affliction. In Chapter 6 the angel explains that burning them as smoke before an afflicted person makes the affliction flee. In Chapter 8 Tobias lays them on incense ashes in the bride-chamber, and the smell drives the demon to Egypt's uppermost parts.

l: bile of the fish, Tobit
s: Tobias is told to carry the bile of the fish in his hand as they near Nineveh. Raphael explains that anointing Tobit's eyes with it will prick them, so that he rubs them and the white films fall away. Tobias rubs it on his father's eyes, and it is the means by which the films peel away.

l: marriage of Tobias and Sarah, Tobit
s: is_required_by law of Moses [Raguel may not marry Sarah to another] The angel proposes that Sarah be given to Tobias as wife, arguing that she is his kinswoman and that the law of Moses requires it, and says it will take place that night, with the celebration after their return from Rages. Tobias fears the fate of Sarah's earlier husbands but is told to burn the fish's heart and liver and to pray with her to God. He comes to love her.

l: Edna, Tobit
s: Edna, wife of Raguel and mother of Sarah, weeps over Tobit's blindness, prepares the chamber, comforts her weeping daughter, and prays that the Lord grant her favor.

l: marriage contract (Tobias and Sarah's), Tobit
s: is_written_by Raguel [written in a book and sealed] After giving Sarah to Tobias, Raguel takes a book, writes a contract, and seals it. The eating begins after this.

l: demon, Tobit
s: A demon that, smelling smoke from burned fish heart and liver, flees to Egypt's uppermost parts, where the angel Raphael binds it.

l: God, Tobit
s: created Adam God is addressed in Tobias's prayer as God of the fathers, with a holy and glorious name, who made Adam and gave him Eve as a helper. Raguel blesses God for gladness and for having dealt with them according to his great mercy, not as he suspected. Raguel also asks him to show mercy to the two only children and to fulfill their lives in health.

l: grave (Raguel's grave), Tobit
s: is_dug_by Raguel [in case Tobias died] Raguel digs the grave at night, saying "Lest he also should die." Once the maidservant reports that Tobias is alive, Raguel commands his servants to fill it, so it goes unused.

l: wedding feast (Tobias and Sarah's wedding feast), Tobit
s: Raguel keeps the wedding feast for fourteen days. Before it ends he swears that Tobias must not leave until all fourteen days are fulfilled, after which Tobias may take half of Raguel's goods and go in safety to his father. The wedding feast is the occasion Tobias wants Gabael to attend, and he stays because Raguel has sworn that he must not depart. Raphael and Gabael rise early and arrive at the feast together, and Tobias blesses his wife.

l: Tobias and Sarah's marriage prayer, Tobit
s: addresses God [as God of our fathers] Tobias rises from the bed and asks his bride to rise and pray for the Lord's mercy on them. He blesses God, recalls that God made Adam and gave him Eve as a helper, and says he takes his sister not for lust but in truth, asking to find mercy and grow old with her. She says "Amen" with him, and they sleep.

l: healing (Raphael's cure of Tobit's household), Tobit
s: Raphael, sent by God, heals Tobit's household. Fish bile rubbed on Tobit's eyes stings, and white films peel away. He sees Tobias, praises God's mercy after scourging, and Nineveh's people marvel while his kindred rejoice. Sarah is also healed.

l: blessing and thanking God, Tobit
s: is good Raphael urges Tobit and Tobias to bless, thank, and magnify God before all the living, and not to be slack in thanking him. He repeats the command to bless God forever and to give thanks as he ascends. Afterward the two confess God's great and wonderful works.

l: children of Israel, Tobit
s: located_among Gentiles [scattered by God] The children of Israel are told to give thanks to God before the Gentiles, among whom he has scattered them. They are told to declare his greatness there because he is their Lord and Father forever. God will scourge them for their iniquities, show mercy again, and gather them out of all the nations.

l: Jerusalem's future glory, Tobit
s: Tobit's foretelling of Jerusalem's future glory: the city built of sapphires, emeralds and precious stones, with pure gold walls, towers and battlements, and streets paved with beryl, carbuncle and Ophir stones. Nations bring gifts to the King of heaven, generations sing rejoicing, and former mourners rejoice.

l: God's scourging and mercy, Tobit
s: God's scourging and mercy is a prayer's theme: no one escapes his hand, and he leads down to the grave and brings up again. He scourges Israel and Jerusalem for iniquities, then shows mercy, gathering the scattered; wholehearted turning to him brings his turning back.

l: house of God, Tobit
s: The house of God in Jerusalem, per Tobit's foretelling, will be burned and left desolate for a time, then rebuilt less grand until times are fulfilled, and finally built forever gloriously.

l: Israelites (Tobit's kindred and people), Tobit
s: will_be scattered on the earth [from the good land] Tobit foretells that his kindred will be scattered on the earth from the good land, but God will have mercy, bring them back, and rebuild Jerusalem. Those who love the Lord God in truth and righteousness will rejoice and show mercy to their kindred, and the Lord will exalt his people.

l: destruction of Nineveh, Tobit
s: Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus capture Nineveh, fulfilling Jonah's prophecy; Tobit trusts it and urges his family to leave, and Tobias, hearing of the destruction before dying, rejoices.

l: Esther (Greek)
s: This is the Greek version of the Book of Esther, told in ten chapters, about how a plot to destroy the Jews of King Ahasuerus's realm is reversed. The central figures are Mordecai, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin serving at Susa; his cousin Esther, whom he raised and who becomes queen; King Ahasuerus; and Haman, the king's favored official and the villain. The text opens with Mordecai's vision of two serpents and conflicting nations, and his exposure of a plot by two chamberlains against the king. Ahasuerus holds great feasts, and Queen Vashti refuses his summons, so on Memucan's advice she is removed. Beautiful virgins are gathered, and Esther, who at Mordecai's command hides her family and country, is loved above all and crowned. Mordecai again uncovers a chamberlains' plot through Esther, and his goodwill is recorded in the royal library. Haman is promoted, and Mordecai alone refuses to bow to him. Enraged, Haman casts lots, which fall on the fourteenth of Adar, offers ten thousand talents of silver, and obtains a decree, sent to 127 provinces, ordering the Jews' destruction. Mordecai mourns and urges Esther to plead with the king, asking who knows whether she became queen for this occasion. She asks the Jews to fast three days, and both she and Mordecai pray to the Lord. Esther goes uncalled before the king, and God changes his anger to gentleness. She invites the king and Haman to two banquets, while Haman, boasting to his wife Zeresh and friends, prepares a fifty-cubit gallows for Mordecai. That night the king, sleepless, learns Mordecai was never rewarded and has Haman honor Mordecai publicly. At the second banquet Esther names Haman as the enemy of her people. The king, finding Haman fallen on her couch, takes this as an assault, and Haman is hanged on his own gallows. Mordecai receives the king's ring and Haman's holdings, and Esther obtains a reversing letter, dated the twenty-third of Nisan, permitting the Jews to defend themselves on the thirteenth of Adar. Many Gentiles become Jews out of fear. On that day the Jews overcome their adversaries, killing five hundred in Susa including Haman's ten sons, three hundred more the next day, and fifteen thousand elsewhere, taking no spoil. Mordecai establishes the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as Purim, named for the lots, a feast of joy and gifts to be kept forever. The final chapter notes Mordecai's high office, then gives his interpretation of the opening dream: the river is Esther, the serpents are Haman and himself, and God ordained two lots. It closes with a colophon saying Dositheus and his son Ptolemeus brought the Purim letter to Egypt, as interpreted by Lysimachus in Jerusalem.

l: King Ahasuerus, Esther (Greek)
s: King Ahasuerus is a great king who reigns from the throne in Susa over 127 provinces stretching from India to Ethiopia. He holds a ring used to seal decrees, a golden sceptre whose extension spares the life of anyone entering uncalled, a robe of fine linen, a horse, servants, noble friends and two chamberlains. He levies a tax on land and sea, and his strength, valour, wealth and glory are recorded in the book of the Persians and Medes. The story shows a powerful but easily swayed ruler whose decrees, once sealed, cannot be countermanded. It opens with Mordecai informing him of a plot, and the chamberlains Gabatha and Tharrha, who are executed, and the matter recorded. In his third year he holds a long feast displaying his wealth, then grows angry when Vashti refuses his summons and follows Memucan's advice in issuing a decree to all provinces. His anger subsides, and he gathers virgins, loves Esther above all, crowns her queen, holds a seven-day banquet and grants a remission of taxes. He then honors Haman above his friends, orders all to bow to him, accepts his accusation against the Jews, and gives him the ring to seal decrees of destruction, with the silver as well. Esther, who has not been called for thirty days, risks appearing uncalled. The king looks at her with anger, but God changes his spirit to gentleness; he embraces her, lays the sceptre on her neck, and offers up to half his kingdom. Unable to sleep, he has the records read, learns Mordecai was never rewarded, and has Haman honor Mordecai. At Esther's feast he learns of the threat to her and her people, reacts with anger at finding Haman on her couch, and orders him hanged on his own gallows. His wrath subsides. He gives Esther Haman's possessions and Mordecai the ring, extends the sceptre, and authorizes writings in his name permitting the Jews to defend themselves. He hears the Susa death toll, permits a second day of killing, and gives Haman's sons' bodies to be hanged. The account ends with his tax levy, the record of his glory, Mordecai as his viceroy, and Esther as the wife he made queen.

l: Vashti, Esther (Greek)
s: Vashti is a beautiful queen who hosted a banquet for the palace women while the king feasted. She refused his summons to be displayed for her beauty on the seventh day, so a decree barred her from the king and gave her royalty to Esther.

l: Mordecai, Esther (Greek)
s: Mordecai is a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Jair (also given as Jairus), living in Susa. He was among the captives carried from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar and serves in the king's palace and courtyard under King Ahasuerus. He raised his foster child Esther as his own and charged her not to reveal her family. Early on he sees a vision of two serpents and the exaltation of the lowly, and he keeps it in his heart. He learns of two chamberlains' plot against the king and reports it; the deed is recorded in the royal library, but he is not rewarded at first. He refuses to bow to Haman, ignoring the officials who question him daily and disclosing that he is a Jew, so as not to set human glory above God's; he worships the Lord God exclusively. Haman's rage turns into a plot against Mordecai and his whole people, and a fifty-cubit gallows is prepared for him on the advice of Zeresh and Haman's friends. Mordecai responds with sackcloth, dust and a cry that an innocent nation is to be destroyed. He sends Hathach a copy of the decree, charges Esther to plead with the king and warns her she and her father's house will perish if she is silent. After she agrees, he organizes the fast and prays. The reversal comes when the king, finding his unrewarded service in the records, has him dressed in royal robes, mounted on the king's horse and paraded through the city. Haman's wife and friends say the living God is with him. The gallows meant for Mordecai is used to hang Haman. Mordecai receives the king's ring, is appointed by Esther over all that had been Haman's, and goes out in royal apparel with a golden crown and purple diadem while Susa rejoices. The king's letter calls him a deliverer and perpetual benefactor. Feared by officials, he writes the account, sends it to all Jews, and with Esther establishes Purim on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as days of feasting and gifts for all generations. He ends as viceroy to Ahasuerus, a great man honored by the Jews and loved by his nation, declaring that these events came from God and interpreting his dream, identifying himself and Haman as the two serpents.

l: Haman, Esther (Greek)
s: Haman, son of Hammedatha, is described in the Greek Esther records as a Bougean (Bugaean), and in the king's and Mordecai's letters as a Macedonian, an alien to the Persians. He is the central antagonist: a man highly honored and exalted by King Ahasuerus, set above all the king's friends, holding the next place to the king, second post and chief ruler in the kingdom. A Haman is also listed among the seven chamberlains who were sent to bring in Vashti. He is called a slanderer, wicked, arrogant, and the enemy of the Jews, of Mordecai, and of Esther's people. The story begins with Haman, honored in the king's sight, seeking to harm Mordecai and his people because of the executed chamberlains. In chapter 3 he is enraged when Mordecai refuses to bow, plots the destruction of all the Jews, casts lots that fall on the fourteenth day of Adar, accuses the Jews before the king as a nation with differing laws, and promises ten thousand talents of silver into the treasury. He receives the king's ring and commands the writing of the decrees sent to the provinces. Mordecai and Esther pray against him; Esther asks that the counsel of Israel's enemies be turned back on themselves and says she has not eaten at his table. In chapter 5 he is invited with the king to Esther's feast and leaves glad, but seeing Mordecai in the court enrages him again. He tells his wife Zeresh and his friends of his wealth and honor, says none of it pleases him while Mordecai remains, and, pleased by their advice, has gallows prepared for hanging Mordecai. In chapter 6 he comes to ask for Mordecai's hanging, but, believing the king wishes to honor himself, proposes the robe, horse and proclamation, and is then ordered to do all of it for Mordecai. He goes home mourning with his head covered, Zeresh and his friends tell him he will assuredly fall, and he is hurried to Esther's banquet. In chapter 7 Esther names him as the wicked enemy. Terrified, he begs her for mercy and falls on her couch, which the king takes as an assault. He is hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. His possessions go to Esther and his ring to Mordecai. The king's letter says he was hanged with his whole family at the gates of Susa, and Mordecai's letter says his calamities fell on himself and he was hanged with his children, his ten sons. Finally, Mordecai's dream interpretation identifies Haman as one of the two serpents, the other being Mordecai.

l: Memucan, Esther (Greek)
s: advises Ahasuerus [proposed decree against Vashti] Memucan told the king and princes that Vashti had wronged not only the king but all the rulers and princes, and that other wives would dishonor their husbands likewise. He advised a royal decree, unalterable under Median and Persian law, barring Vashti from the king and giving her royalty to a better woman. The king and princes were pleased and the king acted on this advice.

l: chamberlains (Gabatha and Tharrha), Esther (Greek)
s: Gabatha and Tharrha, the king's chamberlains and body-guard chiefs, resented Mordecai's promotion and plotted to kill King Ahasuerus; the plot was discovered, and the king examined and hanged them.

l: Susa, Esther (Greek)
s: has_event five hundred men killed by the Jews [plus three hundred more the next day] In Susa the Jews killed five hundred men on the first day, including Haman's ten sons, and the toll was reported to the king. The Jews there assembled again on the fourteenth and killed three hundred more, taking no property. They rested and celebrated on the fourteenth and fifteenth.

l: God, Esther (Greek)
s: God is portrayed as almighty king over all, Overseer and Preserver of all things, and God of Abraham. In Chapter 4, Mordecai and Esther pray to him as their only helper, recalling that he redeemed Israel from Egypt and chose them from all nations as a perpetual inheritance, and ask him to spare his people, turn mourning into gladness, and deliver them from death. In Chapter 10, Mordecai credits God with delivering Israel through signs and wonders, ordaining two lots, one for his people and one for the nations, and vindicating his inheritance.

l: Jews, Esther (Greek)
s: The Jews are a nation scattered among the nations, described by Haman as having laws different from others and disobeying the king's laws. Haman plots their destruction, and the king gives him authority; decrees sent to 127 provinces order their destruction and plunder on a set day in Adar. They respond with crying, lamentation, mourning, sackcloth and ashes, and in Susa assemble and fast three days at Esther's instruction, carried out by Mordecai. All Israel cries out to God, facing death. The reversal comes when a letter calls them sons of the living God who live by just laws, granting them the right to use their own laws, help each other, and defend themselves on the thirteenth of Adar. They gain light, gladness and feasting, and many Gentiles become Jews out of fear. They kill five hundred men in Susa on the first day and three hundred more on the fourteenth, while those elsewhere destroy fifteen thousand, taking no spoil. They rest and celebrate, honor Mordecai, and adopt Purim for all generations, observed on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar with gifts of food to neighbors and portions to the poor.

l: Mordecai's vision, Esther (Greek)
s: is_a dream [seen by Mordecai] Mordecai recalls his dream and says not one detail has failed. He explains its elements: the spring that became a river is Esther, the two serpents are Haman and himself, the nations are those who combined to destroy the Jews, and his nation is Israel. The two lots correspond to the one for God's people and the one for the other nations.

l: conspiracy (against King Ahasuerus), Esther (Greek)
s: A plot by two chamberlains, Gabatha and Tharrha, to kill the king over Mordecai's promotion; Mordecai uncovered it and told Esther, who informed the king; both men were hanged and Mordecai's goodwill recorded.

l: king's feast, Esther (Greek)
s: In his third year, Ahasuerus hosted a feast for friends, Persian and Median nobles, and governors, displaying his kingdom's wealth and glory for 180 days. It was followed by a six-day banquet in the court, lavishly adorned with linen, gold and silver couches, and costly cups, held as the king desired, not by appointed law.

l: Vashti's refusal, Esther (Greek)
s: Vashti's refusal is her disobedience of the chamberlains' summons to come to the king on the banquet's seventh day, leaving Ahasuerus grieved and angry; he then asks his friends and the Persian and Median princes for a legal judgment on what to do.

l: royal decree, Esther (Greek)
s: An unalterable royal decree, proposed by Memucan and written under the laws of the Medes and Persians, bars Vashti from entering the king's presence and gives her royalty to a better woman. Sent to all provinces in their own languages, it aims to make wives honor their husbands.

l: wives of the Persian and Median chiefs, Esther (Greek)
s: is_expected_to dishonor husbands [following Vashti's example, per Memucan] Memucan warned that these women, having heard what Vashti said to the king, would dare to dishonor their husbands in the same way. The decree was meant to ensure that all women, poor to rich, would honor their husbands.

l: Esther, Esther (Greek)
s: Esther is a beautiful orphan, daughter of Aminadab and foster daughter of Mordecai, who becomes queen of King Ahasuerus, replacing Vashti. Brought into the care of Hegai, keeper of the women, she receives purification items and seven maidens. Following Mordecai's charge, she conceals her family and kindred, keeps her manner of life, and fears God. She enters the king in the twelfth month of his seventh year, wins his love beyond all other virgins, and is crowned. She later reports Mordecai's discovery of a conspiracy. When her people, the Jews, are threatened, she is troubled, notes that entering uncalled means death and that she has not been called for thirty days, then resolves to go in despite the law. She asks the Jews to fast, humbles herself in ashes and mourning, and prays to the Lord, her only helper, professing that she abhors her royal crown and has not eaten at Haman's table. On the third day she goes with two maids to the king, faints, is comforted, and invites the king and Haman to two banquets. At the second she asks for her life and her people's life, names Haman as the enemy, and he begs her for mercy. She receives Haman's possessions, appoints Mordecai over them, pleads to reverse Haman's letters, and is authorized to write in the king's name. She asks that the Jews may act the next day and that Haman's sons be hanged. With Mordecai she establishes Purim forever. In Mordecai's interpretation, she is the little spring that became a river, the woman the king married and made queen.

l: Adar, Esther (Greek)
s: Adar is the twelfth month, when the king's letters arrived on the thirteenth, the day of killing; the following days, including the fifteenth in Susa, became rest and joy, turning the Jews' mourning into a holiday.

l: virgins (gathered for the king), Esther (Greek)
s: Chaste, beautiful young virgins, chosen by provincial governors at the servants' suggestion, were gathered into Susa's women's apartment under the king's chamberlain. Each underwent twelve months of purification (six with myrrh oil, six with spices), then went to the king; Esther found most favor and replaced Vashti as queen.

l: Haman's decree of destruction, Esther (Greek)
s: Haman's decree is a royal edict, issued in King Ahasuerus's name and sealed with his ring, ordering the destruction of all Jews, including wives and children, and the plunder of their goods. Haman has the recorders write it on the thirteenth day of the first month, addressed to rulers across 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia in their languages. It sets the fourteenth of Adar as the day, and copies are published in every province. Publication in Susa causes Jewish mourning; Mordecai sends a copy to Esther, who joins him in prayer.

l: fast (Esther's and the Jews' three-day fast), Esther (Greek)
s: lasts three days [no eating or drinking, night and day] Esther tells Mordecai to assemble the Jews in Susa and have them fast for her, with no eating or drinking for three days, night and day, while she and her maidens also fast. She says that afterward she will go in to the king contrary to the law, even if she must die. Mordecai does all that she commanded, and prayers by him and Esther accompany the fast.

l: gallows (Haman's gallows for Mordecai), Esther (Greek)
s: Zeresh and Haman's friends propose a gallows fifty cubits tall on which Mordecai would be hanged in the morning after Haman speaks to the king. The proposal pleases Haman, and the gallows is prepared. Bugathan tells the king that a fifty-cubit gallows has been set up on Haman's property for Mordecai. The king orders Haman hanged on it, and Haman is hanged there.

l: banquet (Esther's banquet), Esther (Greek)
s: Esther invites the king and Haman to a feast she prepares that day, and both attend. At the banquet the king asks her request twice, and she instead asks that they come again the next day to a further feast. Haman is glad to be the only one invited with the king.

l: robe of fine linen (the king's robe), Esther (Greek)
s: Haman proposes that the king's servants bring the robe of fine linen the king wears, to be given to a noble friend to dress the honored man. Haman takes the robe and dresses Mordecai in it.

l: horse (the king's horse), Esther (Greek)
s: Haman suggests the horse the king rides as part of the honor for the man the king loves. He takes the horse and mounts Mordecai on it to go through the city streets.

l: procession honoring Mordecai, Esther (Greek)
s: A procession through city streets honoring Mordecai, who rides the king's horse dressed in the king's fine linen robe. Haman devises it believing it is for himself, but the king orders it for Mordecai, and Haman carries it out, proclaiming honor for whomever the king wishes.

l: Haman's plot to destroy the people (plot against Esther's people), Esther (Greek)
s: Esther exposes the plot to the king, describing it as the sale of her people for destruction, pillage, and genocide, and names Haman as the enemy behind it. The plot ends with Haman's hanging.

l: letters sent by Haman, Esther (Greek)
s: has_purpose destruction of the Jews Esther asks that the letters Haman sent, written for the destruction of the Jews in the kingdom, be reversed. The king's letter instructs the provinces to refuse to obey them.

l: king's letter of reversal, Esther (Greek)
s: A royal decree sealed with the king's ring and addressed to governors of 127 provinces. Written by scribes on the twenty-third of Nisan, it denounces Haman, permits Jews their customs and self-defense on the thirteenth of Adar, and calls for festivity. It threatens noncompliant places with destruction, and was sent by couriers and posted publicly.

l: enemies of the Jews, Esther (Greek)
s: The Jews are permitted to treat their adversaries and those who attack them as they please on the thirteenth day of Adar. The king's letter says that for those who plotted against the king this day is a memorial of destruction, and the Jews are told to be ready to fight their enemies.

l: sons of Haman, Esther (Greek)
s: is_a ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha The ten sons of Haman are named as Pharsannes, Delphon, Phasga, Pharadatha, Barea, Sarbaca, Marmasima, Ruphaeus, Arsaeus, and Zabuthaeus. They were among those killed in Susa, and their property was plundered. At Esther's request their bodies were given to the Jews to be hanged.

l: Purim, Esther (Greek)
s: Purim, meaning "lots," is the observance of the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, named for the lots Haman cast and for the Jews' suffering. Mordecai and Esther confirmed it by letter as a memorial kept forever in every generation, with feasting, gladness, gifts to friends and portions to the poor. It closes with assembly, joy and gladness before God, and with the letter being brought by Dositheus and his son Ptolemeus in the fourth year of Ptolemeus and Cleopatra.

l: killing of enemies (by the Jews), Esther (Greek)
s: has_scale fifteen thousand killed outside Susa [no spoil taken] On the thirteenth of Adar the adversaries of the Jews perished, with no one resisting out of fear. Five hundred were killed in Susa, then three hundred more there the next day at Esther's request, and fifteen thousand elsewhere in the kingdom. The Jews took no spoil except in the first Susa killing, where the sons of Haman's property was plundered.

l: The First Book of the Maccabees
s: This document is a sixteen-chapter historical narrative of the Jewish struggle against Greek (Seleucid) rule, and of the rise of the family of Mattathias. It opens with Alexander's conquests and division of his kingdom, from which comes Antiochus Epiphanes. He plunders the Jerusalem temple, bans sacrifice, the Sabbath and circumcision, sets up an abomination of desolation, and burns the law books. Mattathias, a priest at Modin, refuses to sacrifice, kills a Jew who steps up to do so along with the king's officer, and flees to the hills with his five sons. After a thousand die refusing to fight on the Sabbath, his followers decide to resist even then. He dies naming Simon counselor and Judas Maccabaeus captain. Judas defeats Apollonius, Seron, and the armies of Lysias, Gorgias and others, cleanses and rededicates the temple on 25 Chislev in the 148th year, and founds the eight-day festival of dedication. He campaigns against surrounding Gentiles and rescues Jews in Gilead and Galilee. Antiochus dies confessing his evils at Jerusalem, and his young son Eupator, under Lysias, besieges the sanctuary and then makes and breaks a peace. Under Demetrius, Alcimus, the appointed high priest, and Bacchides persecute the faithful. Judas kills Nicanor, a day made a festival, and seeks a treaty with Rome, which sends a bronze-tablet alliance. Judas falls at Elasa fighting Bacchides, and is buried at Modin. His brother Jonathan becomes leader, makes peace with Bacchides, and judges at Michmash. Courted by rival Seleucid claimants Demetrius and Alexander, he becomes high priest under Alexander and later wins confirmation and territory from Demetrius, then from the young Antiochus and Tryphon. He renews ties with Rome and Sparta, but Tryphon seizes him at Ptolemais and later kills him despite a ransom. Simon buries him at Modin, fortifies Judea, and wins release from tribute in the 170th year. He takes Gazara and the Jerusalem citadel, and is honored by the people as leader and high priest until a faithful prophet arises, with Rome and Sparta renewing friendship. Antiochus, son of Demetrius, first confirms Simon's privileges, then repudiates them and sends Cendebaeus against Judea. Simon's sons Judas and John defeat him. Ptolemy son of Abubus, Simon's son-in-law, murders Simon and two sons at a banquet at Dok in the 177th year and tries to seize the country. John, who survives, kills the men sent to kill him, and the narrative points to the chronicles of his high priesthood.

l: Alexander, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Alexander, son of Philip from Chittim, defeated Darius of the Persians and Medes and reigned in his place over Greece. He fought many battles, took strongholds, killed kings, and collected tribute until he fell sick, divided his kingdom among his servants, and died after twelve years. A king of Syria and Ptolemy's son-in-law, he was accused by Ptolemy, lost his wife, was routed, fled to Arabia, and was beheaded by Zabdiel.

l: Alexander's servants, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Alexander's servants, raised with him from youth, received his kingdom from him while he lived and each ruled in his place. After his death they and their sons crowned themselves for years, multiplying evils on the earth; from them came the sinful root Antiochus Epiphanes.

l: King Antiochus, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: King Antiochus Epiphanes is a ruthless ruler, described as a sinful root from Alexander's servants, son of King Antiochus and a former hostage at Rome. He began reigning in the 137th year of the Greeks from his royal city Antioch. He planned to rule both kingdoms, invaded Egypt, and defeated Ptolemy with a vast army. He then plundered Jerusalem and its temple, decreed that all become one people, appointed overseers, sent a tribute collector to Judah's cities, and enforced pagan worship on pain of death. Angered by Judas's fame, he found his treasury depleted by the dissension he caused, left Lysias in charge with orders to destroy Israel's strength and settle foreigners there, and went to Persia for money. Failing to pillage a rich city in Elymais, he fled to Babylon. Hearing of defeats in Judah, he fell sick with grief, admitted his evils at Jerusalem caused his misfortune, appointed Philip guardian of his young son Eupator, and died in the 149th year.

l: Rome, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Rome is a distant power whose senate receives Jewish envoys. Jonathan's envoys secure renewed friendship and alliance, with letters guaranteeing safe conduct. After Jonathan's death, Rome grieves, then renews the pact with Simon, who sends a gold shield to confirm it. Rome is thereby known as calling the Jews friends, allies and kindred.

l: Israel, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Israel is the people and land whose fortunes are traced through a period of persecution, resistance, and recovery. It begins divided: some embrace Gentile ways, while many suffer the plundered temple, slaughter, captivity, and a decree forbidding its worship and law. Many refuse unclean food and choose death, and exceedingly great wrath falls upon it. Mattathias's company, joined by the Hasidaeans, tears down altars and circumcises boys, and Israel laments his death. Under Judas Maccabaeus, wrath is turned away, nations begin to fear him, and the king orders Israel's strength destroyed. The people resolve to repair their ruins and fight for the holy place. Deliverance at Emmaus leads to thanksgiving and an eight-day yearly feast of the altar's dedication. Israelites in Gilead and Galilee are rescued and brought to Judea, though about two thousand fall at Jamnia through disobedience. Israel mourns Judas and suffers under Bacchides until peace comes and Jonathan begins to judge, later mourned too. Finally Simon makes peace, and Israel rejoices in confirmed liberty.

l: transgressors of the law (Israel), The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Transgressors of the law arose from Israel, persuading many to covenant with the Gentiles, blaming separation for evils. With the king's authorization they adopted Gentile ordinances, built a Jerusalem gymnasium, became uncircumcised, forsook the holy covenant, and sold themselves to evil. Later, a sinful nation of such transgressors was placed in the city of David citadel.

l: Gentiles, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: The Gentiles are hostile neighbors of the Jews who profaned Jerusalem's holy things and took her spoils. They shelter apostate Jews and, angered by the rebuilt altar, plot to destroy Jacob's race, killing Jews in several regions, but are repeatedly defeated by Judas and Simon, though Gorgias's force wins at Jamnia.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Jerusalem, a holy city also called the city of David, is the central place in these records, and its fortunes swing between devastation and restoration. It opens with a gymnasium, then Antiochus enters and plunders it. Two years later it is attacked suddenly after words of peace from his chief collector of tribute. It is spoiled, burned, and its houses and walls are pulled down, and women and children are taken captive. The city of David is fortified as a hostile citadel. The inhabitants flee, the city becomes a habitation of foreigners, and its feasts turn to mourning. Mattathias laments the destroyed city, dishonored temple, and stolen vessels. The city lies empty like a wilderness, with foreigners holding the citadel and the king's forces stationed there. The king's order targets its remnant, and later his army advances on Mount Zion, where the king orders the wall pulled down. The abomination on the altar is pulled down. Conflict continues around it: Bacchides withdraws, and Nicanor's men flee into the city of David, and his head and right hand are hung beside the city after his defeat. Recovery begins under Jonathan, who reads Demetrius's letter publicly, rebuilds the city and walls, and besieges the citadel. Demetrius offers to make the city holy and free, and the status of free is granted by Antiochus's letter. Simon then gathers the people, finishes and fortifies the walls, and takes the citadel. He strengthens the temple hill and lives there. The Spartans' letter is read to the congregation. Simon removes the Gentiles from the citadel in the city of David, cleanses the area around the sanctuary, settles Jews in it, and makes the walls high.

l: Ptolemy, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Ptolemy is the king of Egypt and father of Cleopatra. He first gave her in marriage to Alexander at Ptolemais, becoming his father-in-law. He then entered Syria peacefully, garrisoned cities up to Seleucia, turned on Alexander, gave Cleopatra to Demetrius, and crowned himself over Asia and Egypt. He defeated Alexander, received his head, and died three days later.

l: sanctuary, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: The sanctuary is the holy house of prayer and supplication, chosen by God to be called by his name, containing an altar, lampstand, table, and vessels. Its story is one of desecration, cleansing, and restoration. Early on, Antiochus entered presumptuously and stripped its golden furnishings; a citadel became a place of ambush, innocent blood was shed around it, and the king's letters forbade its offerings and ordered it polluted. It was laid waste like a wilderness, trampled, and held by foreigners. The people cried to heaven and resolved to fight, with Judas preferring death in battle to seeing the holy place suffer. When found desolate, with the altar profaned, gates burned, shrubs in the courts and priests' chambers pulled down, blameless priests cleansed it, carried the defiled stones away, consecrated the courts, and furnished new vessels. High walls were restored, and it withstood a long royal siege until peace was made. Nicanor mocked it and threatened to burn it, but the priests prayed and he fell in battle. Finally Simon glorified it, added to its vessels, removed the citadel's occupants, and took charge of it, with tablets set up in its precinct.

l: citadel (at Jerusalem), The First Book of the Maccabees
s: The citadel in Jerusalem is a hostile fortress housing transgressors of the law and Gentiles, serving as a lurking place against the sanctuary. Its troops continually harassed Israel. Judas besieged it in the 150th year, and some besieged slipped out to complain to the king. Jonathan later besieged it with war engines and asked Demetrius to remove its troops, but received only a conditional promise. Finally Simon blockaded it until its occupants starved and surrendered, cleansed it, and entered in the 171st year with celebration, establishing a yearly festival.

l: Antiochus's decree, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Antiochus's decree commanded his whole kingdom to become one people and forsake their own laws, which all nations accepted. For Jerusalem and Judah it banned offerings, Sabbaths, feasts and circumcision, ordered idol altars and unclean sacrifices, appointed overseers, and made disobedience punishable by death.

l: abomination (Antiochus's, on the altar), The First Book of the Maccabees
s: An abomination of desolation was built upon the altar on the fifteenth of Chislev, 145th year; ten days later sacrifice was offered on the idol altar atop the burnt-offering altar, and idol altars spread through Judah's cities.

l: plundering of the temple, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Antiochus Epiphanes, after defeating Egypt in the 143rd year, presumptuously entered the Jerusalem sanctuary with a great multitude, seized the altar, lampstand, table, vessels, silver, gold and hidden treasures, stripped the temple front's gold, slaughtered many, spoke arrogantly, and left, causing great mourning in Israel.

l: persecution of Jews, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: A persecution of Jews marked by slaughter, captivity, the burning of Jerusalem, forced idol sacrifices, and destruction of the books of the law. Possessing a covenant book or consenting to the law, and circumcising children, were punished by death; many died refusing unclean food and profaning the covenant.

l: Mattathias, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Mattathias is a priest of the sons of Joarib, son of John, living at Modin with five sons. Zealous for the law, he mourns Jerusalem's ruin and refuses the king's officers' honors, then kills an apostate Jew and the king's officer at the altar. He flees to the mountains, leads the resistance, and decides to fight on the Sabbath. He gives his sons a farewell charge, blesses them, dies in the 146th year, and is buried at Modin amid great lamentation.

l: sons of Mattathias, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Mattathias's five sons (John, Simon, Judas Maccabaeus, Eleazar, Jonathan) mourn and flee with their father to the mountains, receive his dying charge to defend the law and covenant, name Simon counselor, and bury him at Modin.

l: John, The First Book of the Maccabees
